modules.title: 01. AWS core services
modules.description: The AWS services almost every job uses: IAM, EC2, VPC, S3, RDS, Lambda and CloudWatch. You learn what each is for, how they connect and how to avoid surprise bills.

lessons.title: IAM, EC2 and VPC: identities, servers and networks
objectives: Set up a safe AWS account: MFA on root, an admin user via IAM Identity Center, a billing alarm.
Launch, connect to and stop an EC2 instance; pick an instance type.
Build a VPC with public and private subnets, route tables, an internet gateway and security groups.

topics.title: Account safety
details: Never use root day to day; enable MFA; create a budget alarm at a small amount; use one region while learning.

topics.title: EC2
details: An instance is a virtual machine from an AMI with a type (CPU/RAM), storage (EBS), a key pair or SSM access, and security groups. Stopped instances still pay for storage.

topics.title: VPC
details: A VPC is your private network (CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/16) split into subnets per availability zone. Public subnets route to an internet gateway; private subnets use a NAT gateway (costs money) or VPC endpoints.

reading.locator: EC2 user guide: 'What is Amazon EC2?', 'Instance types' overview and 'Get started with Amazon EC2' tutorial.

assignment.title: Your first network and server
instructions: Secure the account (root MFA, admin via Identity Center, budget alarm).
In the console, build a VPC with two public and two private subnets across two AZs.
Launch a small instance in a public subnet, install nginx, open only port 80 and SSH/SSM from your IP; then terminate it.
deliverables: Screenshots, a network diagram and notes on each component.
acceptanceCriteria: The web page loads; SSH is not open to the world.
Everything is terminated afterwards.

questions.prompt: What makes a subnet public?
questions.answer: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway.

questions.prompt: Why spread subnets across availability zones?
questions.answer: So one data-centre failure does not take the whole app down.

reviewPrompts: Explain a VPC to a friend.
What still costs money after stopping an instance?

lessons.title: S3, RDS, Lambda and CloudWatch: storage, databases, serverless and monitoring
objectives: Store objects in S3 with lifecycle rules and versioning.
Run a managed PostgreSQL in RDS in a private subnet with backups.
Write a Lambda function triggered by S3 and monitor it in CloudWatch with an alarm.

topics.title: S3
details: Buckets hold objects addressed by keys; storage classes trade price for access speed; lifecycle rules move or delete old objects automatically.

topics.title: RDS
details: AWS runs the database: patches, backups, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas. Keep it private; connect from app servers only.

topics.title: Lambda and CloudWatch
details: Lambda runs code on events with no servers to manage; you pay per request and duration. CloudWatch collects metrics and logs; alarms notify you.

reading.locator: Lambda developer guide: 'What is AWS Lambda?', 'Create your first function' and 'Using Lambda with Amazon S3' tutorial.

assignment.title: Thumbnail pipeline
instructions: Create an S3 bucket; upload of an image triggers a Lambda that writes a thumbnail to another prefix.
Log metadata to a small RDS PostgreSQL (or DynamoDB for zero cost) in a private subnet.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on Lambda errors that emails you; then delete everything.
acceptanceCriteria: Uploading an image produces a thumbnail.
A forced error triggers the alarm.

questions.prompt: When is Lambda a good fit?
questions.answer: Short, event-driven tasks with variable traffic.
questions.explanation: Long-running or steady heavy jobs fit containers better.

questions.prompt: What does Multi-AZ RDS give you?
questions.answer: A standby in another AZ with automatic failover.
questions.explanation: Read replicas are for scaling reads.

reviewPrompts: Choose S3 storage classes for logs.
What would you alarm on for a web API?

modules.title: 02. Linux server administration
modules.description: Run real servers: users and permissions, packages, services with systemd, logs, disks, networking and troubleshooting.

lessons.title: Users, services, logs, disks and troubleshooting on a Linux server
objectives: Manage users, groups, sudo and SSH keys securely.
Run an app as a systemd service with restarts and logs in journald.
Troubleshoot CPU, memory, disk and network problems with standard tools.

topics.title: Access
details: Create a non-root user with sudo; key-based SSH only; disable password login; keep packages patched (apt/dnf).

topics.title: Services
details: A systemd unit sets ExecStart, User, Restart=on-failure and dependencies; `systemctl` starts and enables it; `journalctl -u` shows logs.

topics.title: Troubleshooting
details: top/htop for CPU, free for memory, df/du for disk, ss for ports, curl and dig for connectivity, dmesg for kernel errors. Check the simple things first.

reading.locator: systemd.service man page: Description, the [Service] options ExecStart, Restart, User and the Examples section.

assignment.title: Run a service properly
instructions: On an EC2 instance or local VM, create a deploy user, harden SSH and enable automatic security updates.
Run a small Python or Go API as a systemd service behind nginx; kill the process and show systemd restarts it.
Fill the disk with a test file and practise finding and fixing it; write a troubleshooting runbook.
acceptanceCriteria: Service restarts automatically.
Runbook covers CPU, memory, disk and network.

questions.prompt: Which command shows logs of a systemd service?
questions.answer: journalctl -u <service>.

questions.prompt: Which tool lists listening ports?
questions.answer: ss -tlnp (or netstat).

reviewPrompts: Write a minimal unit file from memory.
Your site is down: what do you check first?

modules.title: 03. Infrastructure as code with Terraform
modules.description: Stop clicking in consoles. Describe infrastructure in code, review it in pull requests and recreate it reliably.

lessons.title: Terraform basics: providers, resources, variables, plan and apply
objectives: Write Terraform for AWS resources and run init, plan, apply and destroy.
Use variables, outputs, locals and data sources.
Read a plan carefully before applying.

topics.title: Workflow
details: `terraform init` downloads providers; `plan` shows changes; `apply` makes them; `destroy` removes everything. Always read the plan.

topics.title: Language
details: Resources create things; data sources read existing things; variables are inputs; outputs are results; locals are named expressions.

topics.title: State
details: Terraform remembers what it created in a state file; never edit it by hand; keep it out of Git because it can contain secrets.

reading.locator: Complete the 'Get Started - AWS' tutorials in order: install, build, change, destroy, define input variables, query data with outputs.

assignment.title: Rebuild your network in code
instructions: Recreate the VPC, subnets, security groups and an EC2 web server from the AWS lesson in Terraform.
Make region, CIDR and instance type variables; output the public URL.
Destroy and re-create it twice to prove it is repeatable.
deliverables: Terraform code in Git with a README.
acceptanceCriteria: `terraform apply` from scratch works with no manual steps.

questions.prompt: What does `terraform plan` do?
questions.answer: Shows what would change without changing anything.

questions.prompt: Why not commit the state file?
questions.answer: It can contain secrets and conflicts between people.

reviewPrompts: Resource vs data source?
What happens if you delete a resource from code?

lessons.title: Modules, remote state, workspaces and Terraform in CI
objectives: Write reusable modules with clear inputs and outputs.
Store state remotely with locking.
Run fmt, validate, plan and security scans in CI with apply after approval.

topics.title: Modules
details: A module is a folder of Terraform you call with inputs; keep them small (network, database, service) and version them.

topics.title: Remote state
details: An S3 backend with locking lets a team share state safely; separate state per environment (dev, prod).

topics.title: CI
details: On pull request: fmt, validate, tflint, checkov, plan posted as a comment. On merge: apply with approval. Use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys.

reading.locator: Terraform docs: 'Modules' overview, 'Backend configuration' and the S3 backend page.

assignment.title: Team-ready Terraform
instructions: Split your code into network and service modules with dev and prod environments.
Move state to S3 with locking.
Add a GitHub Actions pipeline using OIDC to AWS: plan on PR, apply on merge after manual approval.
deliverables: Repository with modules, environments and workflow.
acceptanceCriteria: PRs show a plan; no long-lived AWS keys are stored in GitHub.

questions.prompt: Why use state locking?
questions.answer: To stop two people applying at the same time and corrupting state.

questions.prompt: Why OIDC from CI to AWS?
questions.answer: Short-lived credentials instead of long-lived secret keys.

reviewPrompts: How do you structure environments?
Which checks run before apply?

modules.title: 04. Kubernetes fundamentals
modules.description: Learn Kubernetes step by step on a free local cluster: pods, deployments, services, configuration, storage and debugging, then EKS.

lessons.title: Clusters, pods, deployments and services
objectives: Explain the control plane, nodes and kubectl.
Run apps with Deployments and expose them with Services.
Perform rolling updates and rollbacks.

topics.title: Architecture
details: The API server stores desired state in etcd; the scheduler places pods on nodes; controllers keep reality matching your YAML; kubelet runs containers on each node.

topics.title: Workloads
details: A Pod is one or more containers; a Deployment manages replicas and updates; labels and selectors connect things.

topics.title: Networking
details: A Service gives a stable name and IP: ClusterIP inside, NodePort/LoadBalancer outside; Ingress routes HTTP by host and path.

reading.locator: Kubernetes Basics tutorial modules 1-6 in order (create cluster, deploy, explore, expose, scale, update).

assignment.title: Deploy your API
instructions: Install kind and kubectl; create a cluster.
Deploy one of your containerised APIs with 3 replicas and a Service; reach it with port-forward.
Roll out a new version, then roll back; record `kubectl rollout history`.
acceptanceCriteria: Rolling update has no downtime; rollback works.

questions.prompt: What does a Deployment do?
questions.answer: Keeps a desired number of pod replicas running and manages updates.

questions.prompt: Why use a Service instead of pod IPs?
questions.answer: Pods are replaced and get new IPs; the Service is stable.

reviewPrompts: Explain what happens after `kubectl apply`.
ClusterIP vs LoadBalancer?

lessons.title: Configuration, storage, health checks and resources
objectives: Configure apps with ConfigMaps and Secrets.
Add readiness and liveness probes and resource requests/limits.
Use PersistentVolumeClaims and StatefulSets for stateful apps.

topics.title: Config
details: ConfigMaps for settings, Secrets for sensitive values, mounted as files or env vars; never bake config into images.

topics.title: Health and resources
details: Readiness decides if a pod receives traffic; liveness restarts stuck pods. Requests reserve CPU/memory for scheduling; memory limits kill pods that exceed them.

topics.title: Storage
details: PVCs request storage from a StorageClass; StatefulSets give stable names and volumes for databases.

reading.locator: Kubernetes Concepts: 'Configuration' (ConfigMaps, Secrets, resource management for pods) and 'Storage' (persistent volumes).

assignment.title: Production-ready manifests
instructions: Add ConfigMap, Secret, probes and resource requests/limits to your API.
Run PostgreSQL as a StatefulSet with a PVC; show data survives pod deletion.
Break the readiness probe on purpose and observe traffic stops reaching that pod.
acceptanceCriteria: Data persists across pod restarts.
Failing readiness removes the pod from the Service.

questions.prompt: Readiness vs liveness probe?
questions.answer: Readiness controls traffic; liveness restarts the container.
questions.explanation: Do not make liveness depend on dependencies.

questions.prompt: What happens when a pod exceeds its memory limit?
questions.answer: It is killed (OOMKilled) and restarted.

reviewPrompts: How do requests affect scheduling?
When use a StatefulSet?

lessons.title: Debugging Kubernetes and moving to EKS
objectives: Debug CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending and networking issues.
Create an EKS cluster with Terraform and connect kubectl.
Expose services with an ingress/load balancer controller.

topics.title: Debugging
details: `kubectl describe` shows events; `logs --previous` shows the crash; `get events` sorted by time; `exec` and ephemeral debug containers for network checks.

topics.title: EKS
details: AWS runs the control plane; you choose managed node groups or Fargate; IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA/Pod Identity) give pods AWS permissions.

topics.title: Cost
details: An EKS cluster and its nodes cost money hourly; create, test and destroy in one sitting.

reading.locator: Kubernetes docs: 'Troubleshooting Applications' (debug pods, debug services) under Tasks > Monitoring, Logging, and Debugging.

assignment.title: Break-fix and EKS
instructions: Create five broken deployments (bad image, crash, missing secret, no resources, wrong selector) and fix each, noting the clue.
Create a small EKS cluster with Terraform, deploy your API, expose it, then destroy the cluster.
acceptanceCriteria: Each failure has symptom, clue and fix.
EKS is destroyed afterwards.

questions.prompt: A pod is Pending. Common causes?
questions.answer: Not enough CPU/memory on nodes, unsatisfiable selectors/taints, or unbound volumes.

questions.prompt: How do pods get AWS permissions safely on EKS?
questions.answer: IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) or EKS Pod Identity.

reviewPrompts: What does CrashLoopBackOff mean?
What do you pay for in EKS?

modules.title: 05. Helm and CI/CD pipelines
modules.description: Package Kubernetes apps with Helm and build pipelines that test, scan, build and deploy automatically.

lessons.title: Helm charts: templates, values and releases
objectives: Create a chart with templates and values per environment.
Install, upgrade and roll back releases.
Lint and test charts.

topics.title: Charts
details: Chart.yaml, templates/ and values.yaml; templates use Go templating to fill values; keep logic simple.

topics.title: Releases
details: `helm upgrade --install` applies a chart; `helm rollback` returns to a previous revision; values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml separate environments.

topics.title: Quality
details: `helm lint`, `helm template` to see rendered YAML, and chart tests.

reading.locator: Helm docs: 'Quickstart Guide', 'Using Helm' and the Chart Template Guide 'Getting Started' and 'Values Files'.

assignment.title: Chart your API
instructions: Turn your API manifests into a Helm chart with dev and prod values.
Install, upgrade with a new image tag, and roll back.
Add `helm lint` and a template render check to CI.
deliverables: Chart in Git and command log.
acceptanceCriteria: Chart renders cleanly for both environments.

questions.prompt: What does `helm rollback` do?
questions.answer: Restores a release to an earlier revision.

questions.prompt: Why separate values files?
questions.answer: Same chart, different settings per environment.

reviewPrompts: What belongs in values vs templates?
How do you preview rendered YAML?

lessons.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions: test, scan, build, push and deploy
objectives: Build a pipeline: lint, test, security scan, build image, push to a registry.
Use caching, matrix builds and environments with approvals.
Deploy with progressive strategies (rolling, blue-green, canary).

topics.title: Pipeline stages
details: Fast feedback first (lint, unit tests), then image build tagged with the Git SHA, scan with Trivy, push to ECR/GHCR.

topics.title: Security
details: Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, OIDC to clouds, pinned action versions, protected branches.

topics.title: Release strategies
details: Rolling replaces pods gradually; blue-green switches traffic between two versions; canary sends a small percentage first and watches metrics.

reading.locator: GitHub Actions docs: 'Understanding GitHub Actions', 'Workflow syntax', 'Caching dependencies' and 'Using environments for deployment'.

assignment.title: Full pipeline
instructions: Create a workflow that lints, tests, scans and builds your API image, tagging it with the commit SHA.
Deploy to a kind cluster in CI (or to EKS) with Helm, and run a smoke test.
Write how you would add a canary step.
deliverables: Workflow file and successful run links.
acceptanceCriteria: A failing test or high-severity vulnerability stops the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why tag images with the commit SHA?
questions.answer: Every deployment maps exactly to source code.

questions.prompt: What is a canary release?
questions.answer: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version first.

reviewPrompts: Order the pipeline stages and justify.
How do you secure a pipeline?

modules.title: 06. GitOps with Argo CD
modules.description: Let Git be the source of truth for what runs in your clusters, with automatic sync, drift detection and easy rollbacks.

lessons.title: Argo CD: applications, sync, drift and promotion between environments
objectives: Install Argo CD and deploy apps from a Git repository.
Use auto-sync, self-heal and pruning; detect drift.
Promote releases from dev to prod through pull requests.

topics.title: GitOps idea
details: CI builds images; a Git commit updates the desired version; Argo CD pulls and applies it. Rollback = revert the commit.

topics.title: Argo CD
details: Application resources point to a repo path and cluster; sync status shows differences; self-heal undoes manual changes.

topics.title: Promotion
details: Separate folders or branches per environment; a PR changing the prod image tag is the approval record.

reading.locator: Argo CD docs: 'Overview', 'Getting Started' and user guide pages 'Automated Sync Policy' and 'Sync Options'.

assignment.title: GitOps loop
instructions: Install Argo CD in kind; create a config repo with dev and prod overlays for your Helm chart.
Make CI update the dev image tag automatically; promote to prod by PR.
Change a replica count by hand with kubectl and watch Argo CD revert it.
acceptanceCriteria: Manual drift is reverted.
Rollback works by reverting a commit.

questions.prompt: What is drift?
questions.answer: Differences between what is running and what Git declares.

questions.prompt: How do you roll back in GitOps?
questions.answer: Revert the commit that changed the desired state.
questions.explanation: Git history is the audit log.

reviewPrompts: Push-based CD vs GitOps pull?
Where do secrets go in GitOps?

modules.title: 07. Autoscaling and cloud cost (FinOps)
modules.description: Scale pods and nodes automatically with demand, and keep cloud bills under control with measurement and right-sizing.

lessons.title: HPA, KEDA and Karpenter: scaling pods and nodes
objectives: Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU and custom metrics.
Scale on queue length (and to zero) with KEDA.
Explain node autoscaling with Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler.

topics.title: HPA
details: Replicas = ceil(current replicas x current metric / target). Needs metrics-server and correct resource requests.

topics.title: KEDA
details: Scalers read external sources (SQS, Kafka, Prometheus) and drive the HPA, including scaling to zero when idle.

topics.title: Nodes
details: When pods are Pending for lack of capacity, Karpenter launches right-sized nodes and consolidates empty ones; spot instances save money with interruption handling.

reading.locator: Kubernetes 'Horizontal Pod Autoscaling' page in full, including the algorithm details.

assignment.title: Load-driven scaling
instructions: Load-test your API with k6 and configure an HPA; graph replicas against load.
Add a queue worker scaled by KEDA from a Redis or RabbitMQ queue, including scale-to-zero.
Write how Karpenter would add nodes on EKS, including spot handling.
acceptanceCriteria: Replicas rise and fall with load.
Workers scale to zero when idle.

questions.prompt: Why does HPA need resource requests?
questions.answer: CPU utilisation is calculated as a percentage of requests.

questions.prompt: What can KEDA do that basic HPA cannot?
questions.answer: Scale on external event sources and down to zero.

reviewPrompts: Compute replicas: 4 pods at 90% CPU, target 60%.
Pod vs node autoscaling?

lessons.title: FinOps: tagging, cost visibility, right-sizing and commitments
objectives: Tag resources so costs map to teams and services.
Find waste: idle resources, oversized instances, unattached storage.
Compare on-demand, spot, Savings Plans and reserved capacity.

topics.title: Visibility
details: Cost allocation tags, AWS Cost Explorer and budgets; Kubernetes costs per namespace with tools like OpenCost.

topics.title: Optimisation
details: Right-size from utilisation data, schedule dev environments off at night, delete orphaned volumes and snapshots, use lifecycle rules.

topics.title: Pricing models
details: Spot is cheapest but can be interrupted; Savings Plans discount steady usage for a commitment; on-demand is flexible but most expensive.

reading.locator: FinOps Framework overview: principles, phases (Inform, Optimize, Operate) and capabilities list.

assignment.title: Cost report
instructions: Tag every resource in your Terraform with owner, env and service.
Produce a cost report for your labs (Cost Explorer or estimates from the pricing calculator).
List five optimisations with estimated savings and risks.
deliverables: Tagged Terraform and a one-page cost report.
acceptanceCriteria: Every resource is tagged.
Savings estimates show the calculation.

questions.prompt: When are spot instances a bad fit?
questions.answer: For workloads that cannot tolerate sudden interruption.
questions.explanation: Use for stateless or batch work.

questions.prompt: Why tag resources?
questions.answer: To attribute costs and ownership.

reviewPrompts: Name three sources of cloud waste.
Savings Plan vs spot?

modules.title: 08. Observability and SRE practices
modules.description: Know what your systems are doing: metrics, logs and traces, dashboards, SLOs and alerts that wake people only when users are affected.

lessons.title: Metrics, logs and traces with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry
objectives: Instrument a service with OpenTelemetry and expose Prometheus metrics.
Write PromQL for rate, error ratio and latency percentiles.
Build a Grafana dashboard using the RED and USE methods.

topics.title: Three signals
details: Metrics show trends cheaply; logs explain individual events; traces follow one request across services. Correlate them with trace IDs.

topics.title: PromQL
details: rate(http_requests_total[5m]); error ratio = errors / total; histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) for p99 latency.

topics.title: Dashboards
details: RED for services (rate, errors, duration); USE for resources (utilisation, saturation, errors).

reading.locator: Prometheus docs: 'Overview', 'First steps', then 'Querying basics' and the practices pages on instrumentation and histograms.

assignment.title: Observable service
instructions: Install kube-prometheus-stack in kind.
Instrument your API with OpenTelemetry; export metrics and traces.
Build a RED dashboard and find the slowest endpoint from traces.
deliverables: Dashboard JSON, code changes and findings.
acceptanceCriteria: Dashboard shows rate, errors and p99 latency per endpoint.

questions.prompt: What does RED stand for?
questions.answer: Rate, Errors, Duration.

questions.prompt: Why use histograms for latency?
questions.answer: They allow percentile calculation across instances.

reviewPrompts: Write PromQL for error ratio.
When are traces better than logs?

lessons.title: SLOs, error budgets, alerting and on-call
objectives: Define SLIs and SLOs from user experience.
Use error budgets to balance reliability and speed.
Write burn-rate alerts and on-call runbooks.

topics.title: SLOs
details: SLI: good events / total events (e.g. requests under 300 ms). SLO: target such as 99.9% over 30 days.

topics.title: Error budget
details: 1 - SLO is how much failure is allowed; spending it fast pauses risky releases.

topics.title: Alerting
details: Alert on symptoms users feel with multi-window burn rates; every alert links a runbook; review alert noise regularly.

reading.locator: Google SRE book chapter 'Service Level Objectives' in full.

assignment.title: SLOs for your API
instructions: Define two SLIs and SLOs for your API with reasoning.
Implement burn-rate alerts in Prometheus Alertmanager.
Write runbooks and run a game day where you inject latency and follow them.
deliverables: SLO document, alert rules, runbooks and game-day notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Injected latency fires the right alert and the runbook resolves it.

questions.prompt: What is an error budget for a 99.9% SLO?
questions.answer: 0.1% of events may fail in the window.
questions.explanation: About 43 minutes per 30 days for availability.

questions.prompt: Why alert on symptoms not causes?
questions.answer: Users care about failures they feel; cause alerts are noisy.

reviewPrompts: Pick an SLI for a batch job.
What makes an alert actionable?

modules.title: 09. Resilience and disaster recovery
modules.description: Design systems that survive failures: high availability across zones, backups you have actually restored, multi-region strategies and chaos experiments.

lessons.title: RTO, RPO, DR strategies, backups and chaos experiments
objectives: Set RTO and RPO with the business and choose a DR strategy.
Back up and restore databases and Kubernetes state, and test restores.
Run safe chaos experiments with stop conditions.

topics.title: Targets
details: RTO: how long you can be down. RPO: how much data you can lose. Lower targets cost more.

topics.title: Strategies
details: Backup and restore (cheapest, slowest), pilot light, warm standby, active-active multi-site (fastest, most expensive). Route 53 health checks switch traffic.

topics.title: Testing
details: An untested backup is not a backup. Chaos experiments (AWS FIS, killing pods) prove recovery with guardrails and stop conditions.

reading.locator: DR whitepaper sections 'Disaster recovery options in the cloud' and 'Testing disaster recovery'.

assignment.title: Prove recovery
instructions: Set RTO/RPO for your API and pick a strategy with cost reasoning.
Back up the database, destroy it and restore it in a second region with Terraform; time it.
Kill pods and a node in your cluster during load and record user-visible impact.
deliverables: DR plan, timed restore evidence and chaos results.
acceptanceCriteria: Measured restore time meets or explains the RTO gap.

questions.prompt: RTO vs RPO?
questions.answer: RTO is maximum downtime; RPO is maximum data loss.

questions.prompt: Why must chaos experiments have stop conditions?
questions.answer: To halt automatically if harm exceeds limits.

modules.title: 10. AI infrastructure: GPUs and model serving
modules.description: Run AI workloads on Kubernetes: GPU nodes, drivers and monitoring, plus scalable LLM and model serving.

lessons.title: GPU nodes, drivers, scheduling and GPU monitoring
objectives: Explain how containers access GPUs (drivers, container toolkit, device plugin).
Request GPUs in pods and isolate GPU nodes with taints.
Monitor GPU utilisation and memory with DCGM.

topics.title: Stack
details: Node driver -> NVIDIA container toolkit -> Kubernetes device plugin (or GPU operator installs all of it) -> pods request nvidia.com/gpu.

topics.title: Scheduling
details: Taint GPU nodes so only GPU jobs land there; use node selectors; consider time-slicing or MIG to share GPUs.

topics.title: Monitoring and cost
details: DCGM exporter metrics: utilisation, memory, temperature. Idle GPUs are expensive; scale them down.

reading.locator: Kubernetes 'Schedule GPUs' page in full; then NVIDIA Container Toolkit overview.

assignment.title: GPU-ready cluster design
instructions: Write Terraform for an EKS GPU node group with taints and labels (apply only if you have budget; otherwise plan only).
Write a pod spec requesting one GPU with tolerations, and a DCGM exporter dashboard plan.
Estimate hourly cost and a scale-to-zero approach.
acceptanceCriteria: Pod spec schedules only on GPU nodes.
Cost estimate shows the calculation.

questions.prompt: How does a pod request a GPU?
questions.answer: With resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 1 (via the device plugin).
questions.explanation: Whole GPUs unless sharing is configured.

questions.prompt: Why taint GPU nodes?
questions.answer: To keep ordinary pods off expensive GPU nodes.

reviewPrompts: Draw the GPU software stack.
How do you cut idle GPU cost?

lessons.title: Serving models and LLMs: vLLM, KServe, autoscaling and load testing
objectives: Serve an open model with vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server.
Deploy models with KServe including canary rollouts.
Load-test serving and measure tokens per second, time to first token and cost per request.

topics.title: vLLM
details: Continuous batching and paged attention give high throughput; it exposes an OpenAI-compatible API.

topics.title: KServe
details: InferenceService resources handle autoscaling (including to zero) and traffic splitting for canaries.

topics.title: Metrics
details: Time to first token, inter-token latency, throughput, queue depth and GPU memory; scale on queue depth, not CPU.

reading.locator: vLLM docs: 'Quickstart' (offline inference and OpenAI-compatible server) and 'Metrics'.

assignment.title: Serve and measure
instructions: Run a small open model with vLLM (CPU or a free/cheap GPU notebook).
Write KServe manifests with a 90/10 canary between two model versions.
Load-test with concurrency 1, 8 and 32; chart TTFT and throughput.
deliverables: Commands, manifests and a benchmark chart.
acceptanceCriteria: Benchmark lists hardware, model, settings and results.

questions.prompt: Why scale LLM servers on queue depth rather than CPU?
questions.answer: GPU work is the bottleneck; CPU does not reflect load.

questions.prompt: What is time to first token?
questions.answer: Delay until the first generated token arrives.

reviewPrompts: How does continuous batching help?
Plan a canary for a new model.

modules.title: 11. Well-Architected reviews and cloud certifications
modules.description: Review architectures like a senior engineer and prepare the certifications cloud recruiters look for: AWS Solutions Architect Associate and CKA.

lessons.title: Well-Architected reviews and an AWS SAA + CKA study plan
objectives: Run a Well-Architected review across the six pillars.
Plan AWS Solutions Architect Associate and CKA study with hands-on practice.
Present infrastructure projects clearly in a portfolio.

topics.title: Six pillars
details: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability; each has questions and best practices.

topics.title: Certifications
details: SAA tests architecture choices across AWS services; CKA is a hands-on terminal exam: practise kubectl speed, troubleshooting and cluster maintenance.

topics.title: Portfolio
details: Terraform repos with diagrams, runbooks, SLOs, cost and DR evidence show real skill.

reading.locator: Well-Architected Framework: 'The pillars of the framework' and the design principles for each pillar.

assignment.title: Review and plan
instructions: Do a Well-Architected review of your own project; list high-risk issues and fixes.
Write a 10-week plan covering SAA then CKA with weekly labs and practice exams.
Update your infrastructure repository READMEs with diagrams and evidence.
deliverables: Review document, study plan and README updates.
acceptanceCriteria: Each pillar has at least one finding and action.

questions.prompt: Name the six Well-Architected pillars.
questions.answer: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, sustainability.
questions.explanation: Use them as a review checklist.

questions.prompt: What kind of exam is the CKA?
questions.answer: A hands-on, performance-based exam in a live terminal.

reviewPrompts: Which pillar is weakest in your project?
How will you practise for CKA?

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
Cloud labs can cost money: set a billing alarm before you start, use free tiers, and destroy every lab with `terraform destroy` when finished.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Run and administer Linux servers and core AWS services, and describe all infrastructure in Terraform.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A Terraform-built VPC, server and database you can create and destroy on demand.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Package, deploy and update applications on Kubernetes with Helm, CI/CD and GitOps.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A service delivered from Git to a cluster automatically with safe rollbacks.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Scale, observe and keep systems reliable while controlling cost.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Autoscaling, dashboards, SLO alerts, a cost report and a tested disaster-recovery plan.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Run AI workloads on GPU infrastructure and prepare for cloud certifications.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A GPU-aware model-serving deployment and a certification plan.
